claims.text: TaVCrW is considered in disordered BCC solid and liquid states.
TaVCrW exhibits SRO with a stabilization energy of approximately 2–3 meV/atom.
Electronic excitations near the Fermi level may affect TaVCrW.
Replacing EAM and TI with a DFT-trained MTP and FEP will reduce computational cost by more than 80%.
The MTP+FEP method will agree with TOR-TILD to within 0.5 meV/atom.
Accurate reproduction of the ab initio phase-space distribution by the MTP enables FEP to replace TI.
SRO in TaVCrW produces distinctive structure in the high-frequency VDOS that the MTP must reproduce.
In SRO HfNbTaTiZr, high-frequency VDOS structure arises from optical bands associated with HfTi and TiZr clusters.
The MTP captures an enthalpic DAPB penalty associated with disrupting local SRO in TaVCrW.
The SRO-related DAPB penalty modifies the Gibbs free-energy barrier during the solid–liquid phase transition.
FEP can compute the solid–liquid free-energy difference through work or overlap sampling and thereby avoid linear coupling-parameter integration.
Sufficient phase-space overlap is required for the proposed FEP calculation to remain accurate.
A supercell containing more than 100 atoms is sufficient to capture the relevant TaVCrW SRO clusters or correlation length without artificial periodicity effects.
The method is applicable over 2000–2400 K only if that range does not induce magnetic fluctuations absent from MTP training.
Failure to reproduce the SRO-associated high-frequency VDOS features will cause an FEP error exceeding 0.5 meV/atom.
A free-energy discrepancy of 0.5 meV/atom is equivalent to a melting-temperature discrepancy below 10 K.
Standard GGA-PBE/LDA underbinding and overbinding rules are inaccurate for V and Cr at 0 K.
Neglected high-temperature magnetic fluctuations may alter the liquid free-energy landscape.
MoNbTa is a simpler benchmark alloy with known SRO characteristics suitable for comparing TOR-TILD against MTP+FEP.

contradictions.description: The 0.5 meV/atom threshold is alternately described as melting-temperature accuracy, a difference in melting temperature, and a free-energy difference. Melting temperature must be reported in temperature units unless an explicit thermodynamic conversion is defined.
